doc.title: Bobby Shew interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 1, 2020

title: Studio brotherhood lost to ego; too many notes
summary: Shew describes players manipulating call lists, the earlier brotherhood, and ties it to education and Coleman Hawkins's remark about knowing what not to play.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: Smith on this session?” The contractor’d say, “Why is there a problem?” He’d say, “Well I don’t want to say anything bad about those guys you know …” He’s already said it. The contractor would say, “Well who do you want?” And he’d say well can you get my friend here and this other friend of mine. Because we went to school together, or we have the same teacher or something like that. And then Dalton Smith and Bobby Shew are getting a cancellation you see. And this kind of stuff happens and you get a couple of egomaniacal idiots who start to try to manipulate other people’s right to put beans and rice on the table and provide new shoes for their kids. And we’re all in this thing together. Back in the early days, when I first started doing sessions it was a really good brotherhood. People — this one guy would be sick, his wife would be sick, we’d all throw in dates just so he could make some money to help pay for the medical bills or something. And everybody was a brotherhood to try to look out for each other and nobody would ever backstab anybody. But it was like the rock & rollers that got into it, those kind of guys got a different attitude you know. I think when we started this conversation we were talking about the emotional relationship with the music, the human part of this whole thing. And when you get into it when it’s only a money thing and it’s only an ego thing and only, hey you see I’m on this record, I’m on that record, do you see that’s me playing this, that’s me playing that you know. And you get into all of that the whole thing, the game changes. And it becomes like you know you’ve got to keep your back to the wall. There were certain people you just don’t want to be around. And that’s a sad thing. It’s a real horrible thing. But I think why, in my opinion for whatever that’s worth, I think an awful lot of this goes back to what I was saying to you about the problems in the educational system is they make it more and more and more about the perfection — don’t miss any notes kind of thing, and they change the priorities around so it’s all about ego and money and not missing any notes, and see how high I can play. And I hear guys now and I heard a video just two or three hours ago, somebody sent me a video of a trumpet player, a young trumpet player and I listened to him, God he’s got fingers and chops like you can’t believe. But it makes absolutely no sense whatsoever. It’s like, it’s like a million notes for what reason. And it reminded me of a lecture that I have on cassette. It’s an interview with Coleman Hawkins, and, by an English guy when Coleman was over in Britain and this guy interviewed him. And Coleman says on the cassette, he says, “You know I spent my entire life trying to figure out what not to play.” And it’s kind of like as you grow older and so forth you start to — I go back and listen to things I recorded thirty or forty years ago and I’m thinking oh God what was I thinking you know. Yeah, too many notes.
